Lawrence v. Texas. In June 2003, the Supreme Court ruled six to three to decriminalize consensual same-sex relations nationwide, striking down anti-sodomy laws in fourteen states. Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote the majority opinion, which began by directly overturning the 1986 precedent of Bowers v. Hardwick. Kennedy wrote that Bowers was not correct when decided and is not correct today. The case struck down a Texas anti-sodomy law that criminalized consensual same-sex conduct but not identical conduct between heterosexual couples. The majority held that the liberty interest protected by the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause encompasses the right to engage in consensual same-sex conduct. Justice Scalia's dissent warned that the ruling would logically lead to recognition of same-sex marriage, a prediction that proved accurate within twelve years. The decision invalidated sodomy laws in thirteen other states that still had them on the books, though most had been unenforced for years. Lawrence marked a dramatic reversal from Bowers, signaling the Court's fundamentally evolving view on LGBTQ equality over a seventeen-year period. The decision established that LGBTQ people possess constitutional dignity interests in their intimate relations and personal autonomy, laying the groundwork for subsequent victories in cases like Obergefell and Bostock.
